usage: Treatment of severe infections caused by penicillin-susceptible organisms, including neurosyphilis, endocarditis, bacteremia, meningitis, and severe streptococcal infections.
symptoms: Injection site reactions, nausea, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include severe anaphylaxis, Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in syphilis, neurotoxicity/seizures at high doses, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of mild-to-moderate susceptible bacterial infections, including streptococcal pharyngitis, tonsillitis, and mild skin and soft-tissue infections.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, epigastric distress, rash; serious risks include acute hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Long-acting intramuscular treatment for syphilis (primary, secondary, and latent), yaws, and secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever.
symptoms: Injection site pain, erythema; serious risks include fatal inadvertent IV administration (cardiorespiratory arrest), severe anaphylaxis, and Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.

usage: Intramuscular treatment of moderately severe infections caused by penicillin-susceptible organisms, including uncomplicated pneumonia, erysipelas, and neurosyphilis adjunct.
symptoms: Injection site pain, rash, chills; serious risks include Hoigné syndrome (procaine toxicity with agitation, confusion, seizures on accidental IV injection), severe anaphylaxis, and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of susceptible bacterial infections, including selected ear, nose and throat, respiratory, skin and genitourinary infections; also used in specific combination regimens for Helicobacter pylori.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, rash; serious risks include severe allergic reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including selected respiratory, gastrointestinal, urinary and other infections.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, rash; serious risks include allergic reactions, severe skin reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Oral prodrug of ampicillin used for susceptible upper and lower respiratory tract, urinary tract, and skin and soft-tissue infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, maculopapular rash; serious risks include severe allergic reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Pivaloyloxymethyl prodrug of ampicillin used in selected jurisdictions for respiratory, ear, nose, throat, and urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, heartburn, diarrhea; serious risks include carnitine depletion with prolonged use, severe hypersensitivity reactions, and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Phthalidyl ester prodrug of ampicillin indicated for susceptible respiratory tract, urinary tract, and soft-tissue infections.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, skin rash; serious risks include acute anaphylaxis and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Historical semi-synthetic aminopenicillin previously indicated for susceptible respiratory, urinary, and skin infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, allergic rash; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and superinfections (limited current clinical availability).

usage: Prodrug of ampicillin historically used for human infections and in veterinary medicine for bovine mastitis.
symptoms: Gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include allergic anaphylaxis; largely obsolete in human clinical practice.

usage: Historical penicillinase-resistant penicillin previously used for susceptible staphylococcal infections; obsolete in routine therapy and now primarily an in vitro resistance benchmark.
symptoms: Interstitial nephritis (hematuria, fever, eosinophilia), hypersensitivity reactions, bone marrow suppression, and C. difficile colitis; obsolete due to high nephrotoxicity.

usage: Treatment of documented or suspected penicillinase-producing staphylococcal infections, including bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and skin/soft-tissue infections.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, injection site pain or phlebitis; serious risks include severe neutropenia, acute interstitial nephritis, hypokalemia, and severe allergic reactions.

usage: Treatment of infections caused by penicillinase-producing staphylococci, including respiratory tract, skin and skin structure, and bone infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, rash, elevated transaminases; serious risks include drug-induced hepatotoxicity, acute interstitial nephritis, and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of susceptible staphylococcal infections, including impetigo, cellulitis, folliculitis, and respiratory tract infections.
symptoms: Nausea, epigastric discomfort, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include anaphylaxis, cholestatic jaundice/hepatitis, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Oral treatment of mild-to-moderate susceptible penicillinase-producing staphylococcal infections of the skin, soft tissues, and respiratory tract.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, heartburn, abdominal distress, rash; serious risks include acute allergic reactions, esophagitis, cholestatic jaundice, and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of susceptible penicillinase-producing staphylococcal infections, including cellulitis, impetigo, osteomyelitis, and surgical prophylaxis.
symptoms: Gastrointestinal upset, nausea, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include delayed cholestatic jaundice/hepatotoxicity (especially in elderly patients or long courses) and severe anaphylaxis.

usage: Treatment of confirmed or suspected Gram-negative bacterial infections resistant to conventional beta-lactams, including urinary tract and bloodstream infections (active against many ESBL-producers).
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, injection site discomfort; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions, neurotoxicity at elevated serum levels, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Treatment of susceptible systemic and urinary tract infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Proteus species (availability varies regionally).
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, vein irritation; serious risks include platelet dysfunction/bleeding diathesis, hypokalemia, hypernatremia (high sodium load), and hypersensitivity.

usage: Parenteral antipseudomonal carboxypenicillin historically used for severe systemic, urinary tract, and bone/joint infections caused by Pseudomonas and other Gram-negative bacilli.
symptoms: Hypokalemia, nausea, diarrhea, phlebitis; serious risks include bleeding abnormalities due to platelet aggregation inhibition, seizures at high doses, and severe hypersensitivity.

usage: Extended-spectrum antipseudomonal ureidopenicillin used for serious systemic, intra-abdominal, respiratory, and urinary tract infections caused by susceptible Gram-negative bacteria.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, headache, injection site pain; serious risks include severe hypersensitivity reactions, leukopenia/neutropenia with prolonged therapy, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Extended-spectrum ureidopenicillin historically indicated for serious susceptible bacterial infections of the lower respiratory tract, urinary tract, and abdomen.
symptoms: Gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea, phlebitis; serious risks include bleeding tendencies, hypokalemia, acute interstitial nephritis, and allergic anaphylaxis.

usage: Extended-spectrum ureidopenicillin historically used for serious infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa in lower respiratory, urinary, and intra-abdominal sites.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, local venous irritation; serious risks include bleeding disorders, hypokalemia, leukopenia, and acute hypersensitivity reactions.

usage: Regional antipseudomonal penicillin used in selected Asian markets for susceptible Pseudomonas and Proteus infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site discomfort; serious risks include allergic hypersensitivity reactions, electrolyte disturbances, and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of selected susceptible bacterial infections, including some sinus, ear, respiratory, skin and urinary infections.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, rash; serious risks include allergic reactions, C. difficile-associated diarrhoea and liver injury.

usage: Treatment of susceptible skin and skin structure, intra-abdominal, and gynecological infections caused by beta-lactamase-producing strains.
symptoms: Injection site pain, diarrhea, nausea, rash; serious risks include severe anaphylaxis, cholestatic jaundice/hepatotoxicity, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of selected serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including certain intra-abdominal, skin, pelvic and hospital-acquired pneumonia infections.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, rash, headache; serious risks include allergic reactions, kidney-related concerns in some combinations, blood-count changes and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of moderate-to-severe infections caused by susceptible beta-lactamase-producing isolates, including intra-abdominal, urinary, and respiratory infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site reactions, rash; serious risks include bleeding abnormalities, hypokalemia, liver enzyme elevations, and severe allergic reactions.

usage: Treatment of susceptible upper and lower respiratory tract, urinary tract, skin, and intra-abdominal infections caused by beta-lactamase-producing bacteria.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash; serious risks include acute hypersensitivity reactions, elevated liver enzymes, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of susceptible mild-to-moderate bacterial infections including urinary tract infections, skin and skin structure infections, and streptococcal pharyngitis/tonsillitis.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, dyspepsia, rash; serious risks include severe hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of susceptible respiratory, urinary, biliary, and skin infections, endocarditis, and routine perioperative surgical prophylaxis.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site thrombophlebitis, rash; serious risks include allergic reactions/anaphylaxis, neurotoxicity/seizures in renal impairment, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Treatment of selected susceptible skin and soft-tissue, respiratory, bone and genitourinary infections.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, rash; serious risks include allergic reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of susceptible respiratory tract, urinary tract, and skin infections, and surgical prophylaxis in selected jurisdictions.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Parenteral first-generation cephalosporin historically used for susceptible human infections; widely used in veterinary medicine for intramammary bovine mastitis.
symptoms: Injection site pain, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions; primarily veterinary in current practice.

usage: Parenteral first-generation cephalosporin historically used for severe susceptible Gram-positive and urinary tract infections, and surgical prophylaxis.
symptoms: Severe injection site phlebitis/pain, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include nephrotoxicity (especially in combination with aminoglycosides) and severe hypersensitivity.

usage: First-generation cephalosporin developed for susceptible bacterial infections; obsolete/limited commercial clinical availability.
symptoms: Gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include allergic reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea (non-routine historical agent).

usage: Oral first-generation cephalosporin used in selected European and Asian countries for susceptible respiratory, urinary, and skin infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, rash; serious risks include acute hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of susceptible otitis media, lower and upper respiratory tract infections, urinary tract infections, and skin infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash; serious risks include serum sickness-like reactions (arthralgia, fever, erythema multiforme, especially in pediatric patients) and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Second-generation cephalosporin historically used for susceptible respiratory, urinary, and soft-tissue infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, injection site pain; serious risks include hypoprothrombinemia/bleeding and disulfiram-like ethanol reactions (due to NMTT side chain), and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Cephamycin antibiotic used for susceptible intra-abdominal, gynecological, and surgical prophylaxis, with notable activity against anaerobes including Bacteroides fragilis.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site thrombophlebitis, eosinophilia; serious risks include severe hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of susceptible mild-to-moderate pharyngitis, tonsillitis, otitis media, acute sinusitis, bronchitis, and uncomplicated skin infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rash; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of selected susceptible infections, including certain respiratory, ear, skin and urinary tract infections; formulations have different approved uses.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, rash; serious risks include allergic reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Long-acting parenteral second-generation cephalosporin historically used for susceptible respiratory, bone/joint, and skin infections.
symptoms: Injection site pain, diarrhea, nausea, rash; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Cephamycin antibiotic indicated for susceptible gynecologic, intra-abdominal, and surgical prophylaxis with anaerobic coverage.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, rash; serious risks include hypoprothrombinemia/coagulopathy and disulfiram-like reactions with alcohol (NMTT side chain), and severe hemolytic anemia.

usage: Second-generation parenteral cephalosporin historically used for susceptible lower respiratory tract, urinary tract, and bone infections.
symptoms: Pain at injection site, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Cephamycin indicated for susceptible intra-abdominal, gynecological, urinary, and respiratory infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site pain; serious risks include bleeding/hypoprothrombinemia, disulfiram-like ethanol reactions (NMTT side chain), and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Second-generation cephamycin used in selected regional markets for susceptible intra-abdominal, biliary, and pelvic infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include bleeding tendencies/hypoprothrombinemia (NMTT side chain), hypersensitivity, and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Oral third-generation cephalosporin ester used in Japan and East Asia for susceptible respiratory, dermatological, and urinary infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, rash; serious risks include pivalate-associated carnitine deficiency (in ester form), hypersensitivity, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Investigational/regional oral third-generation cephalosporin developed for susceptible respiratory and urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Gastrointestinal disturbance, diarrhea, rash; serious risks include allergic reactions and superinfections (limited commercial availability).

usage: Treatment of susceptible community-acquired pneumonia, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, acute maxillary sinusitis, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, and skin infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, vaginal moniliasis, nausea, headache, reddish stools (in presence of iron supplements); serious risks include hypersensitivity and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Oral third-generation cephalosporin for susceptible acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, community-acquired pneumonia, pharyngitis, and uncomplicated skin infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, headache, vaginal candidiasis; serious risks include carnitine deficiency with prolonged use (pivoxil ester) and hypersensitivity reactions.

usage: Oral third-generation cephalosporin prodrug indicated in selected jurisdictions for susceptible respiratory tract, ear/nose/throat, and urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, abdominal cramps, headache; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Oral third-generation cephalosporin indicated for susceptible uncomplicated urinary tract infections, otitis media, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, and uncomplicated gonorrhea.
symptoms: Diarrhea, loose stools, abdominal pain, nausea, dyspepsia, flatulence; serious risks include severe allergic reactions/anaphylaxis and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Parenteral third-generation cephalosporin used regionally for susceptible septicemia, respiratory tract, urinary tract, and biliary infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, injection site reactions; serious risks include bleeding/hypoprothrombinemia (NMTT side chain), disulfiram-like ethanol reactions, and hypersensitivity.

usage: Broad-spectrum third-generation parenteral cephalosporin used regionally for susceptible lower respiratory tract and urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, rash, injection site discomfort; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Third-generation antipseudomonal cephalosporin with extensive biliary excretion, used for susceptible biliary, intra-abdominal, and respiratory infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, phlebitis; serious risks include hypoprothrombinemia/bleeding (NMTT side chain, vitamin K reversible), disulfiram-like ethanol reaction, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Treatment of serious susceptible infections including bacterial meningitis, pneumonia, bacteremia, intra-abdominal, bone/joint, and genitourinary infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, injection site inflammation, rash; serious risks include severe anaphylaxis, granulocytopenia, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Third-generation parenteral cephalosporin developed for susceptible Pseudomonas and enterobacterial infections (limited/regional clinical availability).
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, local site irritation; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Oral third-generation cephalosporin for susceptible community-acquired pneumonia, acute otitis media, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, and skin/urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, vaginal fungal infections, abdominal pain, headache; serious risks include severe allergic reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Oral third-generation cephalosporin pivoxil ester used regionally in Japan/Asia for susceptible respiratory, urinary, and otolaryngological infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, loose stools, nausea, rash; serious risks include carnitine deficiency with prolonged pediatric administration and severe hypersensitivity.

usage: Oral third-generation cephalosporin indicated for susceptible acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, acute bacterial otitis media, and pharyngitis/tonsillitis.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, dyspepsia, abdominal pain; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Veterinary-exclusive third-generation cephalosporin indicated for bovine respiratory disease, swine respiratory disease, and equine bacterial infections.
symptoms: Veterinary injection site reactions; strictly NOT approved or indicated for human administration (risk of beta-lactam hypersensitivity upon human occupational exposure).

usage: Parenteral third-generation cephalosporin indicated for susceptible lower respiratory tract, urinary tract, intra-abdominal, and pelvic inflammatory infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site discomfort, rash; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of serious or selected susceptible bacterial infections, including certain respiratory, bloodstream, abdominal, urinary, skin, bone/joint and meningitis infections.
symptoms: Injection-site pain, diarrhoea, rash, changes in blood counts; serious risks include allergic reactions, biliary complications and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Third-generation cephalosporin with potent activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, used for nosocomial pneumonia, febrile neutropenia, cUTI, and meningitis.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site phlebitis, pruritus; serious risks include neurotoxicity (encephalopathy, myoclonus, asterixis in renal impairment), anaphylaxis, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Oxacephem broad-spectrum antibiotic historically used for susceptible Gram-negative bacteremia, meningitis, and intra-abdominal infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site pain; serious risks include severe bleeding diathesis/hypoprothrombinemia, disulfiram reactions (NMTT side chain), and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Treatment of selected moderate-to-severe infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including certain pneumonia, urinary, skin and intra-abdominal infections when used with appropriate companion therapy.
symptoms: Rash, diarrhoea, nausea, fever; serious risks include neurotoxicity (especially with impaired kidney function), allergic reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Fourth-generation parenteral cephalosporin used regionally in Japan for susceptible septicemia, respiratory tract, and intra-abdominal infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, elevated transaminases, rash; serious risks include neurotoxicity in renal impairment, hypersensitivity, and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Fourth-generation cephalosporin used in Europe and other regions for severe hospital-acquired pneumonia, bacteremia, and febrile neutropenia.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site pain, rash; serious risks include neurotoxicity (seizures, encephalopathy in renal failure), severe anaphylaxis, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Veterinary-exclusive fourth-generation cephalosporin indicated for bovine respiratory disease, calf septicemia, and swine respiratory infections.
symptoms: Veterinary injection site reactions; strictly NOT approved or indicated for human administration (potential for beta-lactam hypersensitivity upon human occupational exposure).

usage: Advanced-generation cephalosporin indicated for hospital-acquired and community-acquired pneumonia, with activity against MRSA and susceptible Gram-negative bacilli.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, dysgeusia, headache, vomiting; serious risks include severe hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Advanced-generation cephalosporin indicated for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI) and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP), active against MRSA.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, rash, direct Coombs test seroconversion; serious risks include severe hypersensitivity reactions, agranulocytosis, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Combination agent indicated for complicated intra-abdominal infections (with metronidazole), complicated urinary tract infections, and hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, pyrexia; serious risks include severe hypersensitivity reactions, decreased efficacy in baseline renal impairment (CrCl 30-50 mL/min), and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Siderophore cephalosporin indicated for complicated urinary tract infections and hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by susceptible multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria.
symptoms: Diarrhea, infusion site reactions, elevated transaminases, candidiasis; serious risks include boxed warning for higher all-cause mortality in critically ill patients and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Combination agent indicated for complicated intra-abdominal infections, complicated urinary tract infections, and hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia caused by MDR Gram-negative pathogens.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, constipation; serious risks include central nervous system toxicity/seizures in renal impairment, hypersensitivity, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Treatment of selected serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including certain intra-abdominal, lower respiratory, urinary, skin and gynaecological infections.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash; serious risks include seizures, allergic reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of selected serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including complicated intra-abdominal infections, meningitis in indicated patients and certain skin infections.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, headache, rash or infusion-site reactions; serious risks include seizures (risk increased in some patients), allergic reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Once-daily carbapenem indicated for complicated intra-abdominal, complicated skin/skin structure, community-acquired pneumonia, complicated UTI, and colorectal surgical prophylaxis.
symptoms: Diarrhea, infused vein complication, nausea, headache, vaginitis; serious risks include central nervous system toxicity/seizures, anaphylaxis, and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Carbapenem indicated for complicated intra-abdominal infections and complicated urinary tract infections caused by susceptible pathogens.
symptoms: Headache, nausea, diarrhea, rash, phlebitis; serious risks include increased mortality in ventilator-associated pneumonia (boxed warning/discontinued indication), seizures, and anaphylaxis.

usage: Carbapenem co-administered with betamipron, used regionally in Japan and China for severe susceptible respiratory, urinary, and intra-abdominal infections.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, elevated transaminases; serious risks include seizures, hypersensitivity reactions, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Parenteral carbapenem with high dehydropeptidase-I stability, approved in Japan and China for sepsis, pneumonia, and complicated urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, rash, elevated ALT/AST; serious risks include central nervous system toxicity/convulsions, interstitial pneumonia, and severe hypersensitivity.

usage: Oral carbapenem pivoxil ester used in Japan for pediatric respiratory and ENT infections; investigated globally for complicated urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, loose stools, nausea; serious risks include pivalate-related carnitine deficiency with prolonged use, hypersensitivity reactions, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Investigational parenteral carbapenem developed for multiresistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Gram-negative hospital infections.
symptoms: Gastrointestinal disturbance, rash, injection site irritation; serious risks include hypersensitivity and neurotoxicity (investigational agent; not routine clinical therapy).

usage: Monobactam active against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria (including Pseudomonas); IV formulation for systemic infections; inhaled formulation for cystic fibrosis Pseudomonas management.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash, cough/bronchospasm (inhalation); serious risks include anaphylaxis (rare cross-reactivity with penicillins, except ceftazidime) and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Investigational oral monobactam developed for susceptible Gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, abdominal cramps; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and superinfections (developmental/non-marketed agent).

usage: Parenteral monobactam used regionally in selected countries for susceptible Gram-negative urinary, respiratory, and biliary tract infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, injection site reactions, elevated transaminases; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of selected susceptible bacterial infections, including certain respiratory, skin and sexually transmitted infections.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal pain; serious risks include QT prolongation/abnormal heart rhythm, liver injury and severe allergic or skin reactions.

usage: Treatment of selected susceptible bacterial infections, including respiratory and skin infections; also used in combination regimens for H. pylori.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal pain, altered taste; serious risks include QT prolongation, liver injury, severe allergic reactions and important drug interactions.

usage: Treatment of selected infections caused by susceptible bacteria; specific uses depend on formulation and indication.
symptoms: Nausea, abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea; serious risks include QT prolongation/arrhythmias, liver injury and allergic reactions.

usage: Semi-synthetic macrolide approved in Europe and Australia for susceptible respiratory tract, ENT, genital, and skin infections.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, diarrhea, headache; serious risks include QT prolongation, cholestatic hepatotoxicity, and hypersensitivity reactions.

usage: Ketolide antibiotic historically approved for community-acquired pneumonia of mild to moderate severity caused by susceptible organisms.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, dizziness, dysgeusia, visual disturbances/blurred vision; serious risks include boxed warnings for severe fatal hepatotoxicity, visual impairment, and exacerbation of myasthenia gravis.

usage: Oral macrolide prodrug of erythromycylamine historically indicated for mild-to-moderate respiratory and skin infections.
symptoms: Abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache; serious risks include QT prolongation, cardiac arrhythmias, and severe hypersensitivity (withdrawn/discontinued in many markets).

usage: 16-membered natural macrolide approved in Europe and Japan for susceptible respiratory, ENT, dermatological, and dental infections.
symptoms: Nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, anorexia; serious risks include hepatotoxicity, allergic reactions, and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: 16-membered macrolide complex used regionally in human medicine and widely in veterinary feed/medicine for susceptible Gram-positive and mycoplasmal infections.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions and hepatotoxicity (limited human regulatory authorization in US/EU).

usage: 16-membered macrolide used regionally in Japan and Europe for susceptible upper and lower respiratory infections and dermatologic infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, anorexia, rash; serious risks include hepatotoxicity, QT interval prolongation, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Historical macrolide antibiotic previously indicated for susceptible staphylococcal and streptococcal infections; largely obsolete in modern human therapeutics.
symptoms: Gastrointestinal distress, nausea, diarrhea; serious risks include cholestatic jaundice, severe allergic reactions, and drug-drug interactions (discontinued/historical).

usage: 16-membered macrolide used for susceptible oral/dental and respiratory infections, and specifically as primary therapy for congenital toxoplasmosis prevention in pregnancy.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, paresthesia; serious risks include QT prolongation, acute cholestatic hepatitis, and hypersensitivity reactions.

usage: Triacetyl ester prodrug of oleandomycin historically used for susceptible respiratory infections and as an adjunct in severe corticosteroid-dependent asthma.
symptoms: Abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea; serious risks include severe cholestatic jaundice/hepatotoxicity, potent CYP3A4 inhibition with toxic drug interactions.

usage: Veterinary-exclusive 16-membered macrolide indicated for swine dysentery, bovine respiratory complex, and canine/feline chronic enteropathy.
symptoms: Veterinary gastrointestinal irritation, rectal edema in swine; strictly NOT approved for human medical therapy (fatal cardiovascular toxicity reported on accidental human parenteral exposure).

usage: Narrow-spectrum macrocyclic antibiotic indicated for the treatment of Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea in adults and pediatric patients.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, anemia; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions (low systemic absorption minimizes systemic toxicity).

usage: Investigational fluoroketolide developed for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia and uncomplicated gonorrhea.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, infusion site pain; serious risks include transient transaminase elevations, hepatotoxicity concerns, and visual disturbance (not commercially approved).

usage: Investigational ketolide developed for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia and post-exposure prophylaxis for inhalation anthrax.
symptoms: Dysgeusia, nausea, diarrhea, headache; serious risks include potential ketolide-class hepatotoxicity and QT interval prolongation (not commercially approved).

usage: Treatment of selected infections caused by susceptible bacteria; use is restricted for some uncomplicated infections when safer alternatives are suitable.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort, headache; serious risks include tendon injury/rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, QT prolongation and worsening of myasthenia gravis.

usage: Treatment of selected susceptible bacterial infections, including certain pneumonia, sinus, urinary and skin infections; reserve for some conditions when alternatives are appropriate.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhoea, headache, insomnia; serious risks include tendon injury, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, QT prolongation and worsening of myasthenia gravis.

usage: Treatment of selected susceptible bacterial infections, including certain respiratory and skin infections; not suitable for every infection site.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhoea, dizziness; serious risks include QT prolongation, tendon injury, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects and worsening of myasthenia gravis.

usage: Fluoroquinolone indicated for the treatment of acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic bronchitis and mild-to-moderate community-acquired pneumonia.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, rash, headache, dizziness; serious risks include boxed warnings for tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, QT prolongation, and high incidence of maculopapular rash.

usage: Fluoroquinolone indicated for susceptible mild-to-moderate urinary tract, respiratory tract, skin, and sexually transmitted infections (also ophthalmic/otic solutions).
symptoms: Nausea, insomnia, headache, dizziness, diarrhea; serious risks include boxed warnings for tendonitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS toxicities, and QT prolongation.

usage: Oral fluoroquinolone historically indicated for susceptible uncomplicated and complicated urinary tract infections, prostatitis, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis prophylaxis.
symptoms: Nausea, headache, dizziness, abdominal cramps, diarrhea; serious risks include boxed warnings for tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, and QT prolongation.

usage: Oral fluoroquinolone historically indicated for susceptible uncomplicated urethral/endocervical gonorrhea and urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Nausea, dizziness, headache, insomnia, dyspepsia; serious risks include boxed warnings for tendinitis, peripheral neuropathy, CNS toxicity, and severe theophylline toxicity due to CYP1A2 inhibition.

usage: Fluoroquinolone indicated topically for bacterial conjunctivitis; systemic formulations withdrawn globally due to severe dysglycemia.
symptoms: Ophthalmic: conjunctival irritation, keratitis, eye pain; Systemic (withdrawn): severe life-threatening hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia (dysglycemia boxed warning), tendon rupture, and QT prolongation.

usage: Fluoroquinolone historically indicated for susceptible urinary tract infections and acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis.
symptoms: Headache, nausea, dizziness, pronounced photosensitivity; serious risks include severe phototoxicity/blistering on sunlight exposure, tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS toxicities.

usage: First-generation synthetic quinolone historically indicated for susceptible uncomplicated urinary tract infections caused by Gram-negative bacilli.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, rash; serious risks include visual disturbances, intracranial hypertension (papilledema in children), hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency, and cartilage erosion.

usage: First-generation quinolone historically indicated for the treatment and prophylaxis of susceptible uncomplicated urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal cramps, dizziness, headache; serious risks include hypersensitivity reactions, phototoxicity, and CNS stimulation (withdrawn/discontinued in most regions).

usage: Pyridopyrimidine quinolone antibiotic historically used in Europe and Asia for susceptible acute and recurrent urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Gastrointestinal upset, nausea, epigastralgia, rash; serious risks include phototoxicity, CNS excitation, and tendinopathy (restricted or withdrawn in the European Union).

usage: First-generation quinolone historically used for urinary tract infections in humans; predominantly used in veterinary aquaculture and agricultural horticulture.
symptoms: Nausea, insomnia, dizziness, restlessness; serious risks include CNS excitation/seizures, cartilage toxicities; obsolete/restricted in human clinical medicine.

usage: First-generation fluoroquinolone used primarily in veterinary medicine (poultry, cattle, aquaculture); historically used in some regions for urinary infections.
symptoms: Veterinary reactions; human: nausea, diarrhea, dizziness; serious risks include phototoxicity, ocular toxicity, tendinopathy, and chondrotoxicity; withdrawn/restricted in human use.

usage: Fluoroquinolone approved in France and selected jurisdictions for susceptible serious urinary, respiratory, bone/joint, and hepatobiliary infections.
symptoms: Nausea, epigastric pain, headache, insomnia; serious risks include high incidence of tendinitis and Achilles tendon rupture, severe phototoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS toxicity.

usage: Broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone historically approved in selected countries for susceptible urinary, respiratory, and enteric infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, insomnia, dizziness, severe phototoxicity; serious risks include pronounced phototoxic skin reactions, CNS excitation, tendon rupture, and QT prolongation (largely discontinued).

usage: Broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone historically indicated for community-acquired pneumonia and acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, dizziness; serious risks include severe phototoxicity (blistering erythema) and pronounced QT interval prolongation/torsades de pointes; withdrawn or discontinued globally.

usage: Fluoroquinolone approved in Japan for susceptible respiratory, urinary, hepatobiliary, and otorhinolaryngological infections.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, rash; serious risks include acute kidney injury/interstitial nephritis, thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity, and tendonitis.

usage: Oral fluoroquinolone approved in Korea and Japan for susceptible uncomplicated and complicated urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Nausea, headache, dizziness, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort; serious risks include tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, and QT prolongation.

usage: Non-zwitterionic fluoroquinolone indicated for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI) and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP), active in acidic environments.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, transaminase elevations; serious risks include boxed warnings for tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS toxicities (has lower phototoxicity and QT risk).

usage: Non-fluorinated topical quinolone cream indicated for the topical treatment of impetigo due to Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes in patients 2 months of age and older.
symptoms: Infantile seborrheic dermatitis, application site erythema, pruritus; serious risks are negligible due to virtually undetectable systemic absorption.

usage: Chlorofluoroquinolone ophthalmic suspension indicated exclusively for the topical treatment of bacterial conjunctivitis caused by susceptible isolates.
symptoms: Conjunctival redness, blurred vision, eye pain, eye pruritus, headache; serious risks are limited to local ocular hypersensitivity (no systemic fluoroquinolone toxicities).

usage: Oral prodrug of ulifloxacin approved in Southern Europe and Japan for susceptible acute lower urinary tract infections, chronic bronchitis, and bacterial sinusitis.
symptoms: Epigastric pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache; serious risks include tendinitis/tendon rupture, phototoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and hypersensitivity reactions.

usage: Parenteral fluoroquinolone approved in Japan for susceptible bacteremia, pneumonia, chronic respiratory infections, complicated UTI, and pelvic peritonitis.
symptoms: Injection site reactions, nausea, diarrhea, elevated transaminases; serious risks include seizures, tendinitis/tendon rupture, acute kidney injury, and hypersensitivity.

usage: Treatment of selected infections caused by tetracycline-susceptible bacteria; use depends on organism and clinical indication.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhoea, photosensitivity; serious risks include severe allergic reactions and effects on developing teeth/bone in certain age groups.

usage: Treatment of selected susceptible bacterial infections, including certain respiratory, skin, tick-borne and sexually transmitted infections; also used for malaria prevention in specified circumstances.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhoea, photosensitivity, oesophageal irritation; serious risks include severe allergic/skin reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea.

usage: Treatment of selected susceptible bacterial infections; some formulations are used for acne or specific skin conditions.
symptoms: Dizziness/vertigo, nausea, diarrhoea, skin or tooth pigmentation; serious risks include liver injury, severe skin reactions and drug-induced autoimmune reactions.

usage: Tetracycline antibiotic historically used for susceptible infections; primarily used off-label for the management of chronic SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion).
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, pronounced photosensitivity; serious risks include nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (polyuria, polydipsia), permanent tooth discoloration in children, and azotemia in liver disease.

usage: Natural tetracycline indicated for susceptible respiratory, rickettsial, and urinary infections; widely used in veterinary medicine for livestock bacterial therapy.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, phototoxicity; serious risks include enamel hypoplasia/tooth staining in pediatric patients, hepatotoxicity at high doses, and superinfections.

usage: First discovered tetracycline; used topically/ophthalmically for superficial ocular and cutaneous infections, and heavily in veterinary agriculture.
symptoms: Topical irritation, redness; systemic/veterinary: nausea, diarrhea; serious risks include tooth staining/bone growth inhibition in young subjects and photosensitivity.

usage: Semi-synthetic tetracycline historically indicated for susceptible respiratory, sexually transmitted, and skin infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, abdominal distress, photosensitivity; serious risks include pediatric tooth discoloration/enamel hypoplasia, benign intracranial hypertension, and C. difficile colitis.

usage: Parenteral Mannich-base prodrug of tetracycline historically used for severe susceptible bacterial infections requiring rapid IV/IM administration.
symptoms: Local injection pain/thrombophlebitis, nausea, vomiting; serious risks include permanent pediatric tooth discoloration, azotemia, and severe hypersensitivity.

usage: Tetracycline prodrug bonded to L-lysine, widely approved in Europe and the UK for moderate-to-severe acne vulgaris and susceptible respiratory/genital infections.
symptoms: Nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache; serious risks include photosensitivity, tooth dyschromia in children under 8 years, and benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri).

usage: Topical tetracycline antibiotic historically formulated as a 1% cream for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris.
symptoms: Skin dryness, burning, stinging, erythema, localized contact dermatitis; virtually non-absorbed systemically with low systemic toxicity risk.

usage: First-in-class glycylcycline indicated for complicated skin and skin structure infections, complicated intra-abdominal infections, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, abdominal pain; serious risks include boxed warning for increased all-cause mortality, pancreatitis, and permanent pediatric tooth discoloration.

usage: Synthetic fluorocycline antibiotic indicated for the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections caused by susceptible Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic pathogens.
symptoms: Infusion site reactions, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, phlebitis; serious risks include permanent pediatric tooth discoloration, bone growth inhibition, pancreatitis, and hypersensitivity.

usage: Aminomethylcycline antibiotic available in oral and IV formulations for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) and acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI).
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, headache, elevated transaminases, diarrhea; serious risks include increased mortality in CABP clinical trials, permanent tooth discoloration in children, and hypersensitivity.

usage: Narrow-spectrum tetracycline-class antibiotic indicated exclusively for the oral treatment of inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne vulgaris.
symptoms: Nausea, dizziness, headache, fatigue, diarrhea; serious risks include permanent pediatric tooth discoloration, photosensitivity, pseudotumor cerebri, and embryofetal toxicity.

usage: Treatment of selected serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, usually with specialist oversight and monitoring.
symptoms: Nausea or injection-site effects may occur; serious risks include kidney injury, hearing/balance damage and neuromuscular effects.

usage: Treatment of selected serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, usually with specialist oversight and monitoring.
symptoms: Nausea or injection-site effects may occur; serious risks include kidney injury, hearing/balance damage and neuromuscular effects.

usage: Aminoglycoside historically indicated for serious Gram-negative bacteremia and second-line therapy for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
symptoms: Tinnitus, vestibular vertigo, elevated creatinine, nausea; serious risks include boxed warnings for irreversible ototoxicity (auditory damage), nephrotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade.

usage: Aminoglycoside formulated topically for skin/wound infections, and orally for bowel decontamination prior to colorectal surgery and hepatic encephalopathy management.
symptoms: Oral: nausea, diarrhea, malabsorption; Topical: contact dermatitis; serious risks include severe ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity if absorbed systemically across broken skin or denuded mucosa.

usage: Semi-synthetic aminoglycoside approved in Europe and other regions for severe susceptible Gram-negative sepsis, intra-abdominal, urinary, and respiratory infections.
symptoms: Decreased urine output, elevated BUN/creatinine, dizziness, tinnitus; serious risks include nephrotoxicity, irreversible ototoxicity (vestibular/cochlear), and neuromuscular blockade.

usage: Treatment of selected serious susceptible bacterial infections; inhaled and ophthalmic formulations have specific uses.
symptoms: Depending on route, cough or airway irritation, nausea, or eye irritation may occur; systemic exposure can cause kidney injury and hearing/balance damage.

usage: First-in-class aminoglycoside indicated for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (in multi-drug regimens), tularemia, plague (Yersinia pestis), and brucellosis.
symptoms: Paresthesias of the face/mouth, dizziness, nausea; serious risks include boxed warnings for vestibular ototoxicity (permanent loss of balance), cochlear hearing loss, nephrotoxicity, and fetal harm.

usage: Non-absorbed luminal aminoglycoside indicated for intestinal amebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica), adjunct in hepatic coma, and visceral leishmaniasis.
symptoms: Nausea, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, vomiting, steatorrhea; serious risks include systemic nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity if significant absorption occurs in patients with ulcerated mucosa.

usage: Aminocyclitol antibiotic structurally related to aminoglycosides, indicated primarily as an alternative treatment for acute uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis and cervicitis.
symptoms: Injection site soreness, urticaria, nausea, chills, insomnia; serious risks include severe anaphylaxis (lacks significant cochlear and renal toxicity characteristic of classical aminoglycosides).

usage: Next-generation aminoglycoside indicated for complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI), including pyelonephritis, caused by multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae.
symptoms: Decreased renal function, headache, nausea, hypertension, diarrhea; serious risks include boxed warnings for nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuromuscular blockade, and fetal harm.

usage: Natural aminoglycoside isolated from Micromonospora inyoensis, approved regionally for susceptible serious Gram-negative systemic and urinary infections.
symptoms: Azotemia, dizziness, tinnitus; serious risks include irreversible ototoxicity (vestibular and auditory), acute tubular necrosis/nephrotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade.

usage: Semi-synthetic aminoglycoside derivative of kanamycin B, used regionally in Japan for susceptible septicemia, respiratory infections, and urinary tract infections.
symptoms: Oliguria, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine, vertigo; serious risks include cochlear hearing loss, vestibular impairment, nephrotoxicity, and neuromuscular paralysis.

usage: Aminoglycoside antibiotic approved in Japan and parts of Europe for susceptible respiratory, urinary, and surgical Gram-negative and staphylococcal infections.
symptoms: Injection site pain, nausea, tinnitus, transient creatinine elevation; serious risks include ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and hypersensitivity reactions.

usage: Aminoglycoside (neomycin B) used topically for superficial skin, ocular, and external ear bacterial infections.
symptoms: Local cutaneous burning, stinging, erythema, allergic contact dermatitis; serious risks include ototoxicity if instilled into the ear in the presence of a perforated tympanic membrane.

usage: Semi-synthetic aminoglycoside resistant to many aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, approved regionally for susceptible respiratory, urinary, and intra-abdominal infections.
symptoms: Nausea, elevated BUN/creatinine, dizziness; serious risks include irreversible ototoxicity (hearing impairment, vestibular dysfunction) and dose-dependent nephrotoxicity.

usage: Semi-synthetic aminoglycoside derivative of dibekacin, approved in Japan for the treatment of sepsis and pneumonia caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
symptoms: Elevated creatinine, proteinuria, hearing impairment, dizziness; serious risks include acute nephrotoxicity, permanent ototoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade.

usage: Treatment depends on route: oral vancomycin is used for certain intestinal infections; intravenous vancomycin is used for selected serious Gram-positive infections.
symptoms: Oral use may cause nausea or abdominal discomfort; IV use may cause infusion reactions. Serious risks include kidney injury, hearing-related toxicity in some circumstances and severe hypersensitivity.

usage: Glycopeptide antibiotic approved in Europe and internationally for serious Gram-positive infections including complicated skin/soft tissue, bone/joint infections, and MRSA bacteremia.
symptoms: Rash, local injection pain, fever, nausea, bronchospasm; serious risks include nephrotoxicity (lower incidence than vancomycin), ototoxicity, thrombocytopenia, and hypersensitivity.

usage: Bactericidal lipoglycopeptide indicated for complicated skin and skin structure infections (cSSSI) and hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia caused by MRSA.
symptoms: Taste disturbance (metallic taste), nausea, vomiting, foamy urine; serious risks include boxed warnings for increased mortality in baseline renal impairment, nephrotoxicity, embryofetal toxicity, and QT prolongation.

usage: Long-acting lipoglycopeptide administered once weekly for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI) caused by susceptible Gram-positive pathogens, including MRSA.
symptoms: Nausea, headache, diarrhea, vomiting, rash; serious risks include infusion-related reactions (rapid infusion flushing/red man syndrome), hepatotoxicity, and hypersensitivity reactions.

usage: Single-dose long-acting lipoglycopeptide indicated for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI) caused by susceptible Gram-positive isolates, including MRSA.
symptoms: Headache, nausea, diarrhea, limb and subcutaneous abscess, vomiting; serious risks include interference with coagulation tests (falsely prolonged aPTT/PT/INR for up to 120 hours), osteomyelitis, and infusion reactions.

usage: Investigational non-absorbable lipoglycodepsipeptide developed for oral treatment of Clostridioides difficile colitis and VRE gastrointestinal decolonization.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, abdominal distension; serious risks are minimized by negligible systemic bioavailability (investigational agent; not commercially marketed).

common_brand_names: Dalacin C, Cleocin, Clindac A (topical), Evoclin
usage: Treatment of selected serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including certain anaerobic, skin, soft-tissue and bone infections.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal pain, rash; major serious risk is C. difficile-associated colitis, which can be severe.

usage: Lincosamide antibiotic indicated for serious susceptible staphylococcal, streptococcal, and pneumococcal infections in penicillin-allergic patients.
symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, rash; serious risks include boxed warning for severe pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile), cardiorespiratory arrest upon rapid IV bolus, and neutropenia.

usage: Veterinary-exclusive lincosamide indicated for intramammary infusion in dairy cattle for the treatment of clinical and subclinical bovine mastitis.
symptoms: Veterinary udder irritation; strictly NOT approved or indicated for human administration (potential for fatal pseudomembranous colitis upon human exposure).

usage: Treatment of selected infections caused by susceptible Gram-positive bacteria, including certain resistant infections such as MRSA and VRE, according to indication.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, headache, vomiting; serious risks include low blood counts, serotonin syndrome with interacting medicines, optic/peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use and lactic acidosis.

usage: Second-generation oxazolidinone prodrug indicated for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI) caused by susceptible Gram-positive pathogens, including MRSA.
symptoms: Nausea, headache, diarrhea, vomiting, dizziness; serious risks include myelosuppression/thrombocytopenia with extended therapy, peripheral/optic neuropathy, and potential serotonin syndrome.

usage: Investigational bi-aryl oxazolidinone developed for community-acquired pneumonia and complicated skin and skin structure infections.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, headache; serious risks include potential oxazolidinone-class myelosuppression and neuropathy (developmental/non-marketed agent).

usage: Polypeptide antibiotic indicated for acute infections caused by susceptible strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter, and other multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organisms.
symptoms: Decreased urine output, dizziness, flushing, paresthesias; serious risks include boxed warnings for dose-dependent nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis), neurotoxicity (neuromuscular blockade, respiratory arrest).

usage: Reserved for selected serious infections caused by susceptible multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria, with specialist oversight.
symptoms: Numbness/tingling, dizziness or gastrointestinal effects may occur; serious risks include kidney injury and neuromuscular toxicity.

usage: Treatment of selected infections caused by susceptible anaerobic bacteria and certain protozoa; indication depends on the infection.
symptoms: Nausea, metallic taste, abdominal discomfort, headache; serious risks include peripheral neuropathy with certain exposure patterns, seizures/encephalopathy rarely and severe skin reactions.

usage: Second-generation nitroimidazole indicated for trichomoniasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, and bacterial vaginosis in non-pregnant adult women.
symptoms: Metallic/bitter taste, nausea, weakness, dizziness, dyspepsia; serious risks include peripheral neuropathy, convulsions, disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, and potential carcinogenicity.

usage: Single-dose 5-nitroimidazole indicated for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis in female patients and trichomoniasis in adolescent and adult patients.
symptoms: Vulvovaginal candidiasis, headache, nausea, dysgeusia, vomiting, diarrhea; serious risks include potential peripheral neuropathy, disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, and hypersensitivity.

usage: Synthetic nitroimidazole approved in Europe and Asia for susceptible anaerobic bacterial infections, amebiasis, giardiasis, and trichomoniasis.
symptoms: Nausea, metallic taste, epigastric discomfort, drowsiness, dizziness; serious risks include peripheral neuropathy, central nervous system tremors/seizures, and disulfiram-like ethanol reaction.

usage: Treatment of susceptible uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections; not appropriate for kidney infection or systemic infection.
symptoms: Nausea, reduced appetite, headache; urine may darken. Serious risks include lung reactions, liver injury, peripheral neuropathy and haemolysis in susceptible patients.

usage: Treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infection in specified patients and formulations.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, nausea, headache, vaginitis; serious allergic reactions and C. difficile-associated diarrhoea are possible.

usage: Broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotic reserved for serious susceptible infections (such as typhoid fever, bacterial meningitis) when less toxic agents are contraindicated.
symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, glossitis; serious risks include boxed warning for irreversible fatal aplastic anemia, dose-dependent bone marrow suppression, and gray baby syndrome in neonates.

usage: Steroidal antibacterial indicated topically for superficial staphylococcal skin infections (impetigo, folliculitis) and orally/IV in selected countries for severe MRSA osteomyelitis/joint infections.
symptoms: Topical: skin irritation, stinging; Oral/IV: dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhea; serious risks include hepatotoxicity/jaundice, and severe fatal rhabdomyolysis when co-administered with statins.

usage: Treatment of selected serious Gram-positive infections, including certain skin infections and bloodstream/right-sided endocarditis; not indicated for pneumonia.
symptoms: Nausea, diarrhoea, headache, injection-site reactions; serious risks include muscle injury/rhabdomyolysis and eosinophilic pneumonia.

usage: Topical RNA-synthetase inhibitor indicated for impetigo caused by S. aureus/S. pyogenes and intranasal eradication of MRSA colonization in patients and healthcare personnel.
symptoms: Local application site burning, stinging, erythema, pruritus; serious risks include contact dermatitis, secondary fungal infections, and polyethylene glycol vehicle toxicity in extensive open wounds.
